# 2 Chronicles 16 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview

The chapter records the tragic final five years of King Asa's 41-year reign. After 35 years of faithful trust in the Lord — including a great victory over Zerah the Ethiopian (ch. 14) and a national covenant renewal (ch. 15) — Asa now faces a lesser threat from Baasha of Israel and fails the test. He trusts in a pagan king rather than God, rejects prophetic correction, and dies in unbelief. The chapter is a classic warning about not finishing well.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-16/
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-16-commentary

---

## v. 1: "In the thirty-sixth year of Asa's reign, Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah and fortified Ramah to prevent anyone from leaving or entering the territory of Asa king of Judah."

**The chronological problem:** Nearly all commentators note a difficulty here. According to 1 Kings 15:33 and 16:8, Baasha began to reign in Asa's third year, reigned 24 years, and died in Asa's twenty-sixth year — about ten years before the "thirty-sixth year" mentioned here. Ellicott calls the statements "obviously irreconcilable" and argues the most likely solution is a scribal error where "thirty-six" was miscopied for "sixteen" (or "twenty-six"), because the Hebrew letter *yod* (10) and *lamed* (30) looked very similar in ancient script, differing by only two small strokes.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-16.html

Gill similarly notes the difficulty and refers the reader to his notes on 1 Kings 15, where he treats the problem in detail.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-16.html

The PreceptAustin page surveys several solutions: (a) "thirty-sixth year" refers to the kingdom of Judah's existence since the schism (making it Asa's 16th regnal year), a view Keil noted and Thiele popularised — but Dillard objects that no other date in the monarchy is reckoned this way; (b) a copyist's error, preferred by Archer and Edersheim; (c) Gaebelein suggests it refers to the 36th year after the revolt of the ten tribes.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-16-commentary

**Ramah's strategic location:** Ramah (modern er-Râm) lay about 4–5 miles north of Jerusalem on the main north-south ridge route. Baasha's fortification of this city created a blockade that could choke off trade, provisions, and pilgrim traffic to Jerusalem. It was a serious threat, effectively besieging the capital economically.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-16-commentary
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-16/

Piper notes that this crisis came after 35 years of almost total peace. Asa, now older and richer, faced a test he should have met with prayer as he had done earlier, but instead turned immediately to human resources.
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/asas-folly

The Pulpit Commentary (from search excerpt) observes that the parallel account is in 1 Kings 15:17-22, though the Chronicler provides material (especially vv. 7–10) not found in Kings, showing his independent source and his theological purpose for the returned exiles.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/16.htm

---

## v. 2: "So Asa withdrew the silver and gold from the treasuries of the house of the LORD and the royal palace, and he sent it with this message to Ben-hadad king of Aram, who was ruling in Damascus."

Ellicott notes that the Chronicler has "purposely weakened" the parallel statement in 1 Kings 15:18, which says Asa took "***all*** the silver and the gold that were left in the treasures of the house of the LORD." The Chronicler softens the indictment by omitting "all" and "that were left."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-16.html

Trapp observes: "Here good Asa began to decline; which was the worse in him, because in his old age, after so great a victory, and so strict a covenant to cleave close to the Lord."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/2-chronicles-16.html

Mark Boda (cited on PreceptAustin) stresses that for the Chronicler, using the temple treasuries — which the Levites were charged to protect (1 Chr 9:26; 26:20, 22) — was a particularly grievous offence.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-16-commentary

Piper emphasises the irony: "Asa pays the king of Syria (with temple money!) to attack Israel." Instead of crying out to God, he immediately turned to money and political intrigue.
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/asas-folly

---

## v. 3: "Let there be a treaty between me and you, between my father and your father. See, I have sent you silver and gold. Now go and break your treaty with Baasha king of Israel, so that he will withdraw from me."

The Geneva Study Bible (Reformation-era) comments: "He thought to repulse his adversary by an unlawful means, that is, by seeking help from infidels, as they who seek the help of Turks, thinking by it to make themselves stronger."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/2-chronicles-16.html

Gill notes that Asa "trusted to an arm of flesh, and even an Heathen king," relying on Ben-hadad's covenant and promises rather than on the Lord.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-16.html

Ellicott notes the Chronicler has made small verbal changes from the Kings parallel (omitting the word "a present" before "silver and gold," writing the Aramaizing form "Darmeseq" for Damascus, and omitting Ben-hadad's pedigree).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-16.html

EnduringWord comments that Asa used the treasure "to buy the favor of Ben-Hadad of Syria so that he would withdraw support from Israel." Apparently Baasha could not stand against Judah by himself and needed Syrian backing.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-16/

---

## v. 4: "And Ben-hadad listened to King Asa and sent the commanders of his armies against the cities of Israel, conquering Ijon, Dan, Abel-maim, and all the store cities of Naphtali."

Ellicott notes that "Abel-maim" is elsewhere called "Abel-beth-maachah" (as in 1 Kings 15:20); "Abel-maim" may be an early textual mistake. "Store cities" (miskĕnôth) in Chronicles replaces "all Cinneroth, with all the land of Naphtali" in Kings — which Ellicott regards as either a paraphrase or a textual corruption.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-16.html

The plan succeeded in worldly terms: Syria attacked Israel's northern cities, opening a second front that forced Baasha to divert attention. EnduringWord notes that "Asa's mistake wasn't that his plan didn't work — it did eliminate the threat from Israel — but that it succeeded in worldly terms while being fundamentally wrong spiritually."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-16/

---

## v. 5: "When Baasha learned of this, he stopped fortifying Ramah and abandoned his work."

Ellicott notes that the Chronicler's reading "let his work cease" is tautologous compared to Kings' "and dwelt in Tirzah," and attributes the difference to a fault in the Chronicler's manuscript.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-16.html

From a spiritual perspective, Piper observes: "So many times when we rely on ourselves and our own resources, things seem to go well for a season. But things are not well when we have stopped hoping in God and started hoping in what man can do."
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/asas-folly

---

## v. 6: "Then King Asa brought all the men of Judah, and they carried away the stones of Ramah and the timbers Baasha had used for building. And with these materials he built up Geba and Mizpah."

Ellicott says that in 1 Kings 15:22 the parallel reads "King Asa called together all Judah; none was exempted" — the Chronicler modified an obscure sentence. Kings also specifies "Geba of Benjamin." Ellicott notes that Jeremiah 41:9–10 mentions a great cistern Asa made in Mizpah "for fear of Baasha king of Israel," adding a poignant detail about Asa's fear-driven building projects.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-16.html

Gill refers the reader to his notes on 1 Kings 15 for the parallel.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-16.html

---

## v. 7: "At that time Hanani the seer came to King Asa of Judah and told him, 'Because you have relied on the king of Aram and not on the LORD your God, the army of the king of Aram has escaped from your hand.'"

**Who was Hanani?** The Pulpit Commentary and Ellicott both suggest Hanani was probably the father of the prophet Jehu son of Hanani, who later prophesied against Baasha (1 Kings 16:1, 7) and rebuked Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles 19:2). Ellicott notes the use of the older term "seer" (rô'eh) points to an ancient source.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-16.html

**What does "the army of the king of Aram has escaped from your hand" mean?** This is the interpretive crux. Asa thought his enemy was Israel (Baasha). But God's perspective was different: the real enemy was Syria, and God wanted to give Asa victory over both Syria and Israel together. By bribing Ben-hadad to switch sides, Asa lost the opportunity for a far greater victory. EnduringWord explains: "He succeeded in gaining Syria's help against Baasha and Israel, but he failed to see what God saw: that the bigger enemy was Syria, and God wanted to give him victory over the greater enemy."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-16/

Gill concurs: had Asa not solicited Ben-hadad to break his league with Baasha, the Syrian king "would have come with him against Asa, and the Lord would have delivered him to him."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-16.html

The Pulpit Commentary elaborates: if the alliance between Ben-hadad and Baasha had not been broken, "both would surely have been taken in one net" — a decisive victory over the combined forces would have been a "tenfold demonstration of God's judgment."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/16.htm

Ellicott adds that Hanani's words are "in perfect accord with the teachings of the greater prophets" (citing Isaiah 30–31; Jeremiah 17:5; Hosea 5:13 etc.), which favours their authenticity.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-16.html

Piper: "God would not only have protected Asa from Baasha and Israel, he would have given the entire Syrian army into the hand of Asa. But Asa threw it away by trusting in money and intrigue instead of God."
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/asas-folly

---

## v. 8: "Were not the Cushites and Libyans a vast army with many chariots and horsemen? Yet because you relied on the LORD, He delivered them into your hand."

This refers to the great victory of 2 Chronicles 14:9–15, where Zerah the Ethiopian came against Asa with an army of a million men and 300 chariots (14:9). Asa had cried out, "LORD, there is none like you to help… we rely on you" (14:11), and God gave victory.

Gill: "with equal ease could and would have delivered the Syrian army unto him, had he as then trusted in the Lord."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-16.html

Ellicott notes that Cushites and Libyans were banded together in Zerah's great army, just as Syrians and Israelites might have united against Judah — the parallel is exact. He adds that the Hebrew of this verse is "unmistakably the chronicler's own."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-16.html

Piper calls this "the first reason" Asa's trust in man was folly: "God had proved to Asa in the past that when he trusted him, great things happened for his good."
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/asas-folly

---

## v. 9: "For the eyes of the LORD roam to and fro over all the earth, to show Himself strong on behalf of those whose hearts are fully devoted to Him. You have acted foolishly in this matter. From now on, therefore, you will be at war."

This is widely regarded as one of the great verses of the Old Testament. Key interpretive points:

**"The eyes of the LORD roam to and fro":** Ellicott notes the verb "run to and fro" (meshotetot) echoes Job 1:7; 2:2 and Zechariah 4:10, where the identical phrase appears: "the eyes of the LORD, they run to and fro in all the earth." He comments: "The Lord is ceaselessly watchful for occasions of helping the faithful." The Hebrew construction emphasises God's active, eager searching — not passive observation.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-16.html

Trapp noted (cited in EnduringWord): "The Hebrew word for 'run to and fro' signifieth, not to take a light view, but to search narrowly into the nature and the course of things."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-16/

**"To show Himself strong":** The Hebrew verb *hithchazzaq* ("to show oneself strong") occurs 15 times in Chronicles out of 27 total OT occurrences. PreceptAustin notes the fascinating link: the same verb (*chazaq*) was used in Azariah's command to Asa in 2 Chronicles 15:7 ("be strong") and in Asa's obedient response in 15:8 ("he took courage"). Asa lost this divine strengthening when his heart was no longer fully the Lord's.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-16-commentary

**"Those whose heart is fully devoted" (Hebrew *shalem*):** PreceptAustin observes that *shalem* is the same word used in 1 Kings 15:14 to describe Asa's heart as "wholly devoted" to the Lord. So at one time Asa *had* this kind of heart — but hearts are prone to drift.
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-16-commentary

Piper's interpretation (Reformed Baptist): The "heart is blameless" means "wholly relying on him — that's what the context requires." He draws out the theological implication: "It belongs to the very nature of God that he overflow with divine power in the lives of people who trust him. This is right at the heart of what it means to be God." He stresses that this is not a weekend activity for God but what He does "all the time everywhere."
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/asas-folly

Gill explains "perfect" as referring to those "whose graces are sincere and unfeigned, though not complete, nor they free from sin, and who, with the heart, sincerely believe in God." He notes that Asa's heart was said to be perfect in the general bent (1 Kings 15:14), "though there was something lacking in his faith at this time, as there often is in the best of men."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-16.html

Gaebelein (dispensational): "Our hearts are perfect toward Him when we trust Him and are obedient to His Word. Then all His power is with us and for us."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/2-chronicles-16.html

**"You have acted foolishly":** Literally, "Thou hast shown thyself foolish" (Ellicott), echoing 2 Samuel 24:10 and 1 Chronicles 21:8.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-16.html

**"From now on you shall have wars":** The Pulpit Commentary explains that although no specific wars are recorded in Asa's remaining years, the pronouncement refers to the inevitable experience of the kingdom: the king had thrown away the opportunity to neutralise a major enemy, so future wars would rush in. Constable adds that this is part of the Chronicler's "retributive motif": obedience brings blessing, disobedience brings discipline.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/16.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-16.html

F.B. Meyer (cited on PreceptAustin) applies it personally: "We often complain that we are bereft of help, and send off for Benhadad. And all the while the eyes of the Lord are looking pitifully and longingly at us. Nothing would give Him greater pleasure than to show Himself strong on our behalf."
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_chronicles_commentaries

---

## v. 10: "Asa was angry with the seer and became so enraged over this matter that he put the man in prison. And at the same time Asa oppressed some of the people."

**The prison:** Ellicott explains the Hebrew *mahpeketh* ("house of the stocks") literally means "turning" or "distortion" — an instrument of torture by which the body was bent double, hands and feet passed through holes in a wooden frame (cf. Jeremiah 20:2; 29:26; Acts 16:24).
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-16.html

Gill: "in a very strait place, in which he could not turn himself, what we call 'little ease'; some say it was the stocks, others a pillory." He also notes it was a just retaliation that Asa himself later suffered foot disease — "a just retaliation for putting the prophet's feet into the stocks."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-16.html

**"Oppressed some of the people":** The Pulpit Commentary reads this as "crushed" (a stronger verb than "oppressed") and suggests these were people who sympathised with Hanani's message or had independently reached the same conclusion. Ellicott agrees: "Those who sympathised with Hanani. Asa suppressed their murmurs with violence."
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/16.htm
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-16.html

The Geneva Bible observes: "Thus instead of turning to God in repentance, he disdained the admonition of the prophet, and punished him, as the wicked do when they are told of their faults."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/2-chronicles-16.html

Constable notes that 2 Chronicles 16:10 "records the first persecution of a prophet, but many others followed (cf. 1 Kings 22:27; Mark 6:17-18)."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-16.html

EnduringWord: "As a man in compromise and unbelief, the presence of those truly loyal to God was convicting and oppressive to Asa."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-16/

Gaebelein: "Asa showed his true state of soul, when, instead of saying, 'I have sinned,' he began to rage; when instead of beseeching Hanani to pray for him, he put him in prison."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/2-chronicles-16.html

---

## v. 11: "Now the rest of the acts of Asa, from beginning to end, are indeed written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel."

The Pulpit Commentary notes the parallel is 1 Kings 15:23–24, where the source is called "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Judah." The Chronicler's citation of "the book of the kings of Judah and Israel" reflects a later, post-exilic reference work.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/16.htm

Ellicott adds that Kings mentions Asa's "might" and "the cities that he built," which confirms the Chronicler's earlier account of Asa's defensive measures.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-16.html

---

## v. 12: "In the thirty-ninth year of his reign, Asa became diseased in his feet, and his malady became increasingly severe. Yet even in his illness he did not seek the LORD, but only the physicians."

**Nature of the disease:** Gill reports the common view that it was gout. The Hebrew phrase rendered "exceeding great" is literally "went upward" (*ad lema'lah*), which some take to mean the disease spread from his feet to his upper body or bowels — possibly dropsy. A physician cited by Gill (Scheuchzer) thought it an oedematous swelling that moved upward and ended in death.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-16.html

**"He did not seek the LORD, but the physicians":** Several interpretive traditions exist:

1. **The physicians were pagan practitioners using magic:** Ellicott says these "Healers" probably "consisted in the use of magical appliances, such as amulets, charms, and exorcisms, as we may infer from the analogous practices of Babylon and Assyria." Gaebelein concurs: "These were in all probability magicians; who used enchantments."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-16.html
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/2-chronicles-16.html

2. **The sin was not consulting physicians but neglecting God:** Gill clarifies: "his seeking to physicians for help in his disease, perhaps, would not have been observed to his reproach, had he also sought unto the Lord, whom he ought to have sought in the first place; and when he applied to the physicians, he should have implored the blessing of God on their prescriptions."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-16.html

3. **Asa had become a practical secularist:** Piper's reading: "Something tragic had happened in Asa's life. In the 35 years of God's blessing on his reign he had gradually (it seems) become a secular humanist 2,800 years before the term was invented. When there is military threat, you don't think of God, you think of money in the treasury and political alliances and armed forces. When there is a threat to your health, you don't think of God, you think of doctors and medicine."
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/asas-folly

EnduringWord adds that the Bible overall is positive about the role of physicians (citing Colossians 4:14; Acts 28:9; James 5:14–15; 1 Timothy 5:23), but it never endorses trusting physicians *instead of* God.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-16/

The Pulpit Commentary notes the emphatic "and also" (*wegam*): just as in his fear of Baasha he sought Ben-hadad rather than God, so in his illness he sought physicians rather than God — a parallel construction underscoring the pattern.
— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_chronicles/16.htm

The Geneva Study Bible: "God plagued his rebellion and by this declared that it is nothing to begin well, unless we continue to the end, that is, zealous of God's glory and put our whole trust in him."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/2-chronicles-16.html

---

## v. 13: "So in the forty-first year of his reign, Asa died and rested with his fathers."

The parallel in 1 Kings 15:24 adds that he "was buried with his fathers in the city of David his father, and Jehoshaphat his son reigned in his stead."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-16.html

Piper's sombre conclusion: "It seems that Asa never did that [repent]. He carried his folly with him to the grave."
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/asas-folly

---

## v. 14: "And he was buried in the tomb that he had cut out for himself in the City of David. They laid him on a bier that was full of spices and various blended perfumes; then they made a great fire in his honor."

**"His own sepulchres" (plural):** Ellicott explains this indicates a family tomb containing many cells or chambers, hewn out of rock. Like the Pharaohs of Egypt, Asa — a great and powerful king — prepared his own resting place in advance.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-16.html

**The spices and burning:** Gill explains this was not cremation — burning of bodies was not practised among the Jews — but the burning of aromatic spices and woods in great quantity, a customary honour at royal funerals (cf. 2 Chronicles 21:19; Jeremiah 34:5). This continued into Herodian times; Josephus records 500 servants bearing spices at Herod's funeral.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-16.html

Ellicott adds that the "extraordinary amount of spices burnt in his honour" indicates both Asa's distinction as a wealthy monarch and the high esteem his subjects held for him, despite his later failures. He rejects the suggestion (by Zöckler) that the Chronicler was criticising "exaggerated splendour and lavish excess" at the burial; rather, the Chronicler "delighted to dwell on the glory of the ancient kings."
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-16.html

---

## Traditions and Differences

### Reformed / Calvinist (John Piper, DesiringGod.org)

Piper emphasises God's sovereignty and eagerness to show His power: "It belongs to the very nature of God that he overflow with divine power in the lives of people who trust him." He reads "heart is blameless" not as sinless perfection but as "wholly relying on him" — the context determines the meaning. He also stresses that God's chastisement can be turned for good if repentance follows (Romans 8:28), but Asa never repented.
— https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/asas-folly

### Baptist (Gill, 18th-century Particular Baptist)

Gill reads "perfect" heart as "sincere and unfeigned, though not complete, nor they free from sin." He sees Asa's disease as just retribution for putting the prophet's feet in the stocks. He carefully distinguishes that seeking physicians was not itself wrong — the fault was not seeking the Lord *first* and not asking God's blessing on the medical treatment.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/2-chronicles-16.html

### Dispensational / Plymouth Brethren (Gaebelein)

Gaebelein reads the "physicians" as magicians using enchantments and emphasises that Asa never returned to the Lord — "no repentance." He sees the chapter as a picture of the weakness of man and the believer's need for constant faith.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/2-chronicles-16.html

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (EnduringWord, David Guzik)

Guzik emphasises the practical warning about "finishing poorly" and the danger of judging by immediate results rather than true faithfulness. He stresses that Asa's compromise "blinds us to spiritual reality" — Asa missed that Syria was the greater enemy. The commentary is strongly applicational: "Age and time do not necessarily make us better; they only do if we continue to follow God in faith."
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-16/

### Anglican (Ellicott)

Ellicott provides the most detailed textual-critical notes, comparing the Hebrew of Chronicles with Kings, noting the Chronicler's stylistic fingerprints (the verb *hithchazzaq*, the Aramaic forms), and discussing textual corruptions. He is cautious about attributing Asa's physicians to magical practice but thinks the comparison with Babylon and Assyria makes it probable.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-16.html

### Reformation-era (Geneva Study Bible)

The Geneva Bible applies the text directly to contemporary politics: seeking help from Ben-hadad is like "they who seek the help of Turks, thinking by it to make themselves stronger." It sees Asa's imprisonment of the prophet as the typical response of the wicked when reproved.
— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gsb/2-chronicles-16.html
